title: The Cost Blowout

scenario.situation: Mean cost-to-serve per customer jumped 34% last quarter, and finance is drafting an across-the-board price increase to recover margin.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: Leadership assumes serving costs rose broadly across the customer base — a platform-wide efficiency problem.
scenario.question: Did costs actually rise for most customers, or is something else distorting the mean?

decisions.prompt: Finance wants the price increase justified with data. How do you frame the investigation?

options.label: Confirm the mean cost increase over time
options.detail: Pull mean cost-to-serve per customer each quarter and show the trend.
options.consequence: The trend line confirms the mean rose — exactly as leadership believed. But you've only verified the symptom they reported, not diagnosed its cause. The question of *who* drove it remains invisible.
options.divergenceCost: Anchored on leadership's framing and produced a chart that confirms bias without adding insight.

options.label: Examine the full cost distribution across customers
options.detail: Plot the distribution of per-customer costs and compare summary statistics — mean, median, and tail — to see where the change is concentrated.
options.consequence: The distribution reveals something the mean hid entirely: a long right tail of high-cost customers that inflates the average, while the bulk of the base is flat. You now have a real question to answer.

options.label: Benchmark Stackpoint's cost against industry peers
options.detail: Source SaaS infrastructure cost benchmarks and see if Stackpoint is out of line.
options.consequence: External benchmarks take weeks to source and compare apples to oranges. You learn nothing about which customers drove the spike or whether the mean is even representative.
options.divergenceCost: Reached outside when the signal was already in internal data — slow and off-target.

options.label: Audit infrastructure unit costs for price increases
options.detail: Check whether cloud provider rates, egress fees, or compute prices rose this quarter.
options.consequence: Unit costs were flat. You've ruled out one hypothesis but still can't explain the spike — you've spent time on the wrong variable and haven't looked at customer-level heterogeneity at all.
options.divergenceCost: Investigated input costs while ignoring the customer-level demand pattern that drove the change.

decisions.prompt: You segment cost by customer and see the distribution is skewed. Which metric do you use to characterize how widespread the cost increase really is?

artifact.title: Mean cost-to-serve per customer segment — this quarter vs. last
artifact.caption: Mean cost per customer by segment. Segment D looks alarming — but means are sensitive to outliers within each segment. Is this a segment-wide problem or a handful of accounts?

options.label: Mean cost-to-serve across all customers
options.detail: Use the company-wide average cost per customer as the primary metric.
options.consequence: The mean is $187 — up 34%. This validates the finance narrative perfectly. But a handful of extreme spenders can move the mean dramatically while 90% of customers are unchanged. You've measured the outliers, not the base.
options.divergenceCost: Used a mean that outliers dominate — mistook a tail event for a broad trend.

options.label: Median cost alongside the 95th-percentile cost
options.detail: Report the median (typical customer) and the 95th percentile (tail behavior) separately.
options.consequence: The median is $48 — nearly identical to last quarter. The 95th percentile exploded from $190 to $1,840. The cost blowout is entirely a tail phenomenon: a small number of customers running pathological queries, not a platform-wide shift.

artifact.title: Cost distribution summary — this quarter vs. last quarter
artifact.caption: Median cost is flat — typical customers are unaffected. The 95th percentile nearly 10x'd: the mean was being pulled by a small, extreme tail.

decisions.prompt: The median is flat but the tail exploded. A small cluster of customers appears to be running extremely expensive queries. What do you tell leadership?

options.label: "It's a handful of power users abusing the platform — cap their query resources immediately."
options.detail: Name the tail as the cause and prescribe a technical fix.
options.consequence: Confident and action-oriented — but you've called a correlation a cause. Those customers may be on enterprise contracts with legitimate high-volume use cases, or the queries may indicate a missing feature driving inefficient workarounds. Hard caps without investigation could churn high-value accounts.
options.divergenceCost: Prescribed a fix from a correlation without confirming what the tail behavior actually represents.

options.label: "The mean is misleading — median cost is flat, and the spike is concentrated in a small tail. An across-the-board price rise would penalize 95% of customers for a problem they didn't cause. We should identify those accounts, understand whether this is legitimate usage or a bug, and address it at the source before making pricing decisions."
options.detail: Present the distribution finding, challenge the proposed action, and recommend a targeted investigation.
options.consequence: Leadership now understands why the mean was a bad summary statistic for this decision. You've redirected a blunt policy instrument toward a surgical fix, and flagged that the tail's root cause still needs confirmation — protecting both margin and customer relationships.

insight: The mean cost-to-serve spiked because a tiny cohort of customers running pathological queries dominated the average — median cost was flat, meaning most customers were unaffected. An across-the-board price increase would have been a blunt, unfair instrument aimed at a problem that didn't exist for 95% of the base. The lesson: means are distorted by outliers; always read the distribution and locate where a change actually lives before prescribing a remedy.
